Birding in Costa Rica

983bird species present
7species found nowhere else
400+species typically seen on a two week trip
250+winter migrants

Birds When to Go Where to Bird Itineraries Prep FAQ Community Cams

At a glance

Best months
  • December to April at peak
  • May to August for value
  • September to November for the raptor passage
Regions
Sarapiqui and La SelvaTortugueroArenalGuanacaste, Tenorio and the Northern WetlandsMonteverdeThe Central HighlandsSan Gerardo de Dota and the Talamanca HighlandsTurrialba and the Pacuare ValleyThe Southern Caribbean and KekoldiCarara and the Tarcoles RiverManuel Antonio and the Quepos CoastThe Osa Peninsula, Corcovado and Golfo DulceBoca TapadaSan Vito and Coto Brus
Itineraries
San Vito and the Coto Brus5 daysThe Central Highlands and Boca Tapada6 daysThe Quetzal Week7 daysBoth Slopes in Nine Days9 daysThe Raptor Passage10 daysThe Classic Fortnight14 daysThe Full Sweep19 days
Transport
Fly into San Jose (SJO) or Liberia (LIR). Most of the country is self-drive; Tortuguero is reached by boat or light aircraft.

When to Go

Costa Rica is warm all year, so the calendar is set by rain and by migration rather than by temperature. The mountains split the country in two: the Pacific slope is dry from December to April, the Caribbean slope has its clearest spell in September and October. On top of that, over 250 migrant species spend the northern winter here.

Peak

December to April

Dry on the Pacific slope, every northern migrant is in the country, and quetzals are nesting at Dota from February.

Go for Resplendent Quetzal, Jabiru, Great Green Macaw, and the longest trip list of the year.

Trade off The highest prices, and the lodges at Monteverde and San Gerardo de Dota fill first.

Typical daily average
  • Coasts: 25 to 28 °C / 77 to 82 °F
  • Central Valley: 20 °C / 68 °F

Green season

May to August

Rain arrives in the afternoons, mornings stay productive, residents are breeding and singing.

Go for Three-wattled Bellbird display at Monteverde into June, and the best value of the year.

Trade off The migrants have gone north, so the list is shorter.

Typical daily average
  • Coasts: 26 to 28 °C / 79 to 82 °F
  • Central Valley: 21 °C / 70 °F

Passage

September to November

The Caribbean slope has its clearest skies of the year, and millions of raptors pass down the coast on migration.

Go for Raptor passage, Tortuguero at its calmest, Agami Heron.

Trade off The Pacific coast is at its wettest, so build the route around the Caribbean side.

Typical daily average
  • Coasts: 26 to 27 °C / 79 to 81 °F
  • Central Valley: 21 °C / 70 °F

5 days

San Vito and the Coto Brus

San Jose (SJO), San Vito 4 nights, San Jose (SJO) out

Highland forest at 1,200 metres near the Panama border. The trip is based at the Wilson Botanical Garden and the Las Cruces reserve behind it, and the Coto Brus wetlands below hold a different set again.

The Full Sweep

San Jose (SJO), then the classic loop plus Turrialba and Rancho Naturalista country, Tortuguero by boat, the Osa Peninsula, and Cano Negro in the far north

Driving: about 37 hours behind the wheel across the whole route, roughly 1,471 km. Tortuguero is reached by boat from the dock at the end of the road, and many people fly the Osa leg back to San Jose rather than drive it, which takes about eleven hours off the total.

Nineteen days reaches the Osa and the far south as well as everything the fortnight covers. Very few operator itineraries run past eighteen days, so this is the long end.

Sarapiqui and La Selva

Caribbean lowland rainforest, about 90 minutes from San Jose

La Selva Biological Station has kept marked trails and research records here since 1968, so the lowland forest is well documented and easy to walk. It is close to the airport and the dawn activity is high, which is why most trips open here.

  • Habitat: Four thousand acres of lowland Caribbean forest at 40 m against Braulio Carrillo, every age from new growth to primary, joined into one corridor that climbs to the peaks.
  • When: December to April brings the northern migrants and the driest tracks. The Caribbean slope has a second clear spell in September and October.
  • Getting there: From Puerto Viejo de Sarapiquí take Route 4 towards Guápiles for 2.6 km, turn right onto a dirt road and left at the guardhouse. La Selva is 600 m further.
  • Look for: Great Green Macaw, Snowy Cotinga, Sunbittern, Great Curassow, Semiplumbeous Hawk, Bare-necked Umbrellabird, Yellow-throated Toucan, King Vulture
  • National park: Braulio Carrillo National Park
  • Stops:
    • La Selva Biological Station : A research station run by the Organization for Tropical Studies, open to day visitors and overnight guests. It has marked trails, fifty years of records, and the antbirds and Great Green Macaw that made its name.
    • : A ranger station and trailhead inside Braulio Carrillo National Park, on the Guapiles road. The foothill forest sits at 500 metres and is the easiest place to try for Bare-necked Umbrellabird.
    • : A steep public road down to a river gorge off the Vara Blanca route. Bird it slowly from the verge for Sunbittern and the torrent species along the water.
    • : A small private garden of heliconias beside the same road, open for a modest fee. It is the traditional place to look for Snowcap.
    • : A local artist hosts feeder and hide sessions in his own garden, booked directly. Photographers here mention his name first.
  • Also covers: Braulio Carrillo National Park, Cope, at Guapiles, El Tapir, La Selva Biological Station, Puerto Viejo de Sarapiqui, Quebrada Gonzalez, Virgen del Socorro
  • Also watch for: Three-toed and two-toed sloth, collared peccary and mantled howler are all regular on the station trails. Strawberry poison dart frogs are on the leaf litter year round, and most active after rain from May to November.
  • Watch: A Great Green Macaw nest at Sarapiqui streams live on our cams page.

Tortuguero

Canals and coastal rainforest, reached by boat or small plane

Birding is done from a boat along the canals at first light, which puts you level with herons, kingfishers and roosting potoos. Green turtles nest on the beach from July to October.

  • Habitat: A strip of land between lagoon and Caribbean at sea level, with an extensive series of natural canals winding through the forest and no roads anywhere in the area.
  • When: September and October are the clearest months on this coast. Green turtles nest from July to October and the lodges fill with them.
  • Getting there: There are no roads. Lodges arrange transport from San José, and the public river taxi runs from the Pavona boat landing, itself reached by bus from Cariari.
  • Look for: Agami Heron, Sungrebe, Great Potoo, Green Ibis
  • Also recorded in the parks here: Crested Eagle, Short-tailed Nighthawk, Black-collared Hawk, Chestnut-colored Woodpecker, Greater Ani, Lesser Swallow-tailed Swift
  • National park: Tortuguero National Park
  • Stops:
    • : Two narrow side canals. A boat runs to them from the village and they are quieter than the main waterway, and Agami Heron stand along them.
    • : A short steep hill behind the village. Walk it at first light for a view over the whole delta.
    • : Open grass and scrub beside the landing strip, a walk from the village. Seed finches and flycatchers show here that the forest keeps hidden.
  • Also covers: Cano Chiquero and Cano Harold, Cerro Tortuguero, The village airstrip edge, Tortuguero National Park, Tortuguero, Limon
  • Also watch for: Green turtles nest on the beach from July to October and leatherbacks from March to May, both watched only with a licensed guide. Spider monkey, caiman and West Indian manatee are all possible from the canal boats.

Arenal

Volcano foothill forest around La Fortuna

Hanging bridges, fruit feeders and forest trails sit within a short drive of each other, and lowland and foothill species overlap here. It is the easiest region in the country to see a lot of birds without much walking.

  • Habitat: Second growth and remnant forest at 600 m around the skirts of an active cone, continuous westwards into the Monteverde cloud forest, with rich volcanic farmland between.
  • When: December to April for the dry weather and the migrants. May to August keeps productive mornings and puts the residents into song.
  • Getting there: From La Fortuna take the Tilarán road west for 14.2 km, turn left onto a dirt road opposite the police post, and the park entrance is 2 km on.
  • Look for: Crested Guan, Keel-billed Motmot, Great Curassow and, for the lucky, Lovely Cotinga, Yellow-throated Toucan, Scarlet-thighed Dacnis
  • National park: Arenal Volcano National Park
  • Stops:
    • Arenal Observatory Lodge : A lodge below the volcano. Its deck, feeders and trail system are open to day visitors for a fee, so you can bird it without staying.
    • : A quiet gravel road along the south shore of the lake, birded from the verge. Keel-billed Motmot and Lovely Cotinga are the reasons to walk it.
    • : A private trail whose suspension bridges put you level with the canopy, which is where much of the forest activity happens.
    • : Open water and shoreline at the dam. It holds the waterbirds the forest regions never give you.
  • Also covers: Arenal hanging bridges, Arenal Observatory Lodge, Arenal Volcano National Park, La Fortuna, The El Castillo road, The Lake Arenal dam sector
  • Also watch for: Mantled howler and white-faced capuchin along the hanging bridges, coati around the trailheads, and eyelash viper coiled on heliconia. Bat colonies emerge at dusk over the lake all year.

Guanacaste, Tenorio and the Northern Wetlands

Dry forest, cloud forest and seasonal marshes across the north

The northwest is drier and more open than the rest of the country, with dry forest species you will not find elsewhere. Tenorio adds cloud forest, and the Palo Verde and Cano Negro wetlands concentrate waterbirds as the lagoons shrink from January to April.

  • Habitat: Tropical dry forest and seasonal marsh on the northern Pacific slope, with the Tempisque floodplain at Palo Verde and the lagoons and river channels of Caño Negro inland.
  • When: January to March, when the wetlands draw down and the birds concentrate. The dry forest is leafless then, which makes everything easier to see.
  • Getting there: Palo Verde is reached on a long dirt road from Bagaces off Route 1 and is usually birded by boat. Caño Negro is north from Los Chiles near the Nicaraguan border.
  • Look for: Jabiru, Long-tailed Manakin, Turquoise-browed Motmot, Nicaraguan Grackle
  • Also recorded in the parks here: White-fronted Amazon, Blue-vented Hummingbird, Great Curassow, Northern Barred Woodcreeper, Crested Guan, King Vulture
  • National parks: Tenorio Volcano National Park, Rincón de la Vieja National Park, Santa Rosa National Park, Guanacaste National Park, Palo Verde National Park
  • Stops:
    • : A launch trip on the Tempisque river inside Palo Verde National Park, booked locally. Herons, Jabiru and the dry season concentrations are the draw.
    • : A wildlife refuge near the Nicaraguan border. The standard way to bird it is a small boat at dawn, arranged in the village, and from January to March it is the best wetland morning in the country.
    • : The wet Caribbean side of Tenorio Volcano National Park, on a well used trail. It gives a different list from the dry lowlands an hour away.
    • : A working cattle ranch and lodge on the Gulf of Nicoya, open to day visitors. It has dry forest, salt pans and easy White-throated Magpie-Jay.
    • : An active volcano with fumaroles. Dry-to-cloud forest trails leave from the Las Pailas entrance.
  • Also covers: Bagaces, Bijagua, Cano Negro, Ensenada, Guanacaste National Park, La Cruz, Palo Verde boat trip, Palo Verde National Park, Santa Rosa National Park, Tenorio Volcano National Park, The Rio Celeste sector, Tenorio
  • Also watch for: Spider monkey and coati in the dry forest, and American crocodile in the Caño Negro channels. The dry season from December to April concentrates everything at the remaining water, which is what makes it the season to come.

Monteverde

Cloud forest on the continental divide, at about 1,400 metres

Several reserves sit side by side on the divide, with well maintained trails and hummingbird feeders. Quetzals are regular, and Three-wattled Bellbirds display on the ridgelines from March to June.

  • Habitat: Twelve thousand acres of cloud forest at 1,500 m on both slopes of the Cordillera de Tilarán, most of the trail system running along the Continental Divide itself.
  • When: February to April for nesting quetzals. Three-wattled Bellbirds display into June, and the reserve sees more than 300 visitors a day in high season.
  • Getting there: Three roads climb to Santa Elena from Route 1. The middle one turns west just south of the Río Lagarto and runs 33 km of dirt; the northern route through Las Juntas is poor.
  • Look for: Resplendent Quetzal, Three-wattled Bellbird, Black Guan, Prong-billed Barbet, Azure-hooded Jay, Golden-browed Chlorophonia, Collared Trogon and the famous hummingbird galleries, Scarlet-thighed Dacnis
  • Parks and reserves: Monteverde Cloud Forest Biological Preserve (private reserve), Santa Elena Cloud Forest Reserve (community reserve), Children's Eternal Rainforest (private reserve)
  • Stops:
    • Curi-Cancha Reserve : A private reserve with a booking cap, so it stays quiet. It generally gives the best quetzal odds in the area.
    • : The reserve most people mean by Monteverde, on the continental divide. Book the early entry slot.
    • Santa Elena Reserve : A community run reserve, higher and wetter than Monteverde and much quieter in the middle of the day.
    • : The low dry edge of the Children's Eternal Rainforest, a short walk from the village. The bellbirds display here in season.
    • : Farmland and forest edge on the road below the town. Bird it from the roadside for a different set of species.
    • : Working salt pans and mudflat on the gulf. On a falling tide this is the best shorebird ground in the country.
  • Also covers: Bajo del Tigre, Children's Eternal Rainforest, Chomes and the Gulf of Nicoya salt pans, Curi-Cancha Reserve, Monteverde Cloud Forest Biological Preserve, Monteverde Cloud Forest Preserve, Santa Elena Cloud Forest Reserve, Santa Elena Reserve, The San Luis valley
  • Also watch for: Olingo and kinkajou on night walks, glass frogs along the stream margins from May to November, and orange-kneed tarantula in roadside banks. Two-toed sloth is regular in the reserve canopy.

The Central Highlands

Mid elevation forest and coffee country within an hour of the airport

Vara Blanca and Bajos del Toro hold wet mid elevation forest close to San Jose, which makes them a practical first or last night. Coffee farms in the Central Valley add open country species.

  • Habitat: High-elevation forest at 2,400 m around one of the world's most accessible craters, with a 1,300 m wide vent, an acid lake and dwarf forest on the rim.
  • When: December to April for the clearest crater views and the highland endemics. Cloud closes in by mid-morning in most months, so arrive at opening.
  • Getting there: From Alajuela take Route 130 north and uphill for 17.8 km, then right at the T-junction for 10.2 km to the gate. Poás is 45 minutes from the airport.
  • Look for: Sooty-faced Finch, Torrent Tyrannulet, Prong-billed Barbet
  • Also recorded in the parks here: Costa Rican Pygmy Owl, Dark Pewee, Green Thorntail, Orange-billed Nightingale-Thrush, Tropical Screech Owl, White-eared Ground Sparrow, Black-and-yellow Phainoptila
  • National parks: Poás Volcano National Park, Juan Castro Blanco National Park, Irazú Volcano National Park
  • Stops:
    • : A roadside cafe above the Sarapiqui road. Its balcony feeders are open to anyone who buys a coffee, and it is probably the best single hour of hummingbird watching in the country.
    • Bosque de Paz : A private reserve and lodge between Poas and Juan Castro Blanco, open for day visits by arrangement. It has feeders and genuine forest.
    • : High volcano scrub and the crater lookout. It needs a timed booking through SICORE.
    • : The waterfall road down the mountain. Bird it from the pullouts on the way.
  • Also covers: Bajos del Toro, Bosque de Paz, Cinchona, Irazú Volcano National Park, Juan Castro Blanco National Park, The Vara Blanca and La Paz road, Vara Blanca, Heredia
  • Also watch for: Coati and nine-banded armadillo around the waterfall gardens, and the wet mid elevation forest holds a strong amphibian list. Hummingbird feeders here also draw two species of squirrel.

San Gerardo de Dota and the Talamanca Highlands

Oak forest at 2,200 metres, with paramo above

This valley is the most reliable place in Costa Rica for Resplendent Quetzal, and lodge guides track the nest trees and the fruiting wild avocados. Above it, the Cerro de la Muerte paramo, the wet grassland above the treeline, holds highland species shared only with western Panama. Bring warm layers. The ridge above the valley is the Cordillera de Talamanca, the highest ground in the country and the reason the bird list here is the one it is.

  • Habitat: Oak cloud forest in a steep river valley below the Cerro de la Muerte páramo, with wild avocado stands that hold the quetzals and orchard edges below them.
  • When: February to April, when the quetzals nest and are at their most reliable. The valley is cold and wet at any time of year, so pack for it.
  • Getting there: The turning is at km 80 on Route 2, the Interamericana south of Cartago, and the road drops nine kilometres of steep concrete and gravel into the valley.
  • Look for: Resplendent Quetzal, Fiery-throated Hummingbird, Volcano Junco, Timberline Wren, Flame-throated Warbler, Spangle-cheeked Tanager
  • Also recorded in the parks here: Sulphur-winged Parakeet, Yellow-winged Vireo, Barred Becard, Yellow-bellied Siskin
  • National parks: Los Quetzales National Park, Chirripó National Park
  • Stops:
    • : A small paid hide and feeder set-up in the valley, built for photography and equally good for watching. Resplendent Quetzal, Flame-throated Warbler and the highland hummingbirds come in.
    • : Family run properties in the valley, open to visitors for a fee. Their fruiting wild avocados draw quetzals from February to May.
    • : A roadside lodge and cafe on the Interamericana with feeders. Its guides will walk you to a quetzal nest.
    • : The radio towers at the high point of the highway, on open ground above the treeline. Volcano Junco and Timberline Wren live here, and it starts near freezing.
    • : The farm where Alexander Skutch wrote his life's work. It is now a reserve open to visitors and run by the Tropical Science Center.
  • Also covers: Batsu Garden, Cerro de la Muerte paramo, km 89, Chirripó National Park, Los Cusingos, Los Quetzales National Park, Miriam's and the Savegre orchards, Paraiso Quetzal, km 70, San Gerardo de Dota
  • Also watch for: Dice's cottontail and highland squirrel along the valley track, and salamanders under the oak leaf litter after rain. The paramo above holds a very different set of small mammals from anywhere else in the country.

Turrialba and the Pacuare Valley

Caribbean foothills and a whitewater river valley

Rancho Naturalista built the reputation here with its hummingbird feeders, and Snowcap is the bird most people come for. The Pacuare gorge adds river forest and lodges reached by raft.

  • Habitat: Middle-elevation Caribbean-slope forest at 850 m, with feeders and forest trails set among coffee and cane, and the Irazú and Turrialba cones on the skyline.
  • When: December to April carries the migrants and the driest trails. The hummingbird pools are worked in the late afternoon in any month.
  • Getting there: From Turrialba head east on Route 10 for 6 km, then right onto Route 232 towards Tuis. Rancho Naturalista is 11.2 km on, on the left of the paved road.
  • Look for: Snowcap, White-crowned Manakin, Sunbittern, Tawny-chested Flycatcher, Purple-throated Mountaingem, Lattice-tailed Trogon, Scarlet-thighed Dacnis
  • Also recorded in the parks here: Carmiol's Tanager, Spotted Woodcreeper, Pale-vented Thrush
  • National parks: Turrialba Volcano National Park, Tapantí National Park, Barbilla National Park
  • Stops:
    • Rancho Naturalista : A birding lodge whose balcony, hummingbird pools and morning moth light are open to day visitors by arrangement.
    • : A community run reserve on the Caribbean slope, up a rough road. Snowcap and Lattice-tailed Trogon are the birds to come for.
    • CATIE grounds : The grounds of an agricultural research centre outside Turrialba, open to walk. It has lakes, old plantings and a long species list.
    • : A public road descending through coffee and forest fragments. Bird it from the car and the verge.
  • Also covers: Barbilla National Park, CATIE grounds, El Copal, Rancho Naturalista, Siquirres, Tapantí National Park, The Tuis valley road, Turrialba Volcano National Park
  • Also watch for: Neotropical river otter on the Pacuare, poison dart frogs on the forest floor, and Central American agouti on the lodge trails. Basilisk lizards run the river margins all year.

The Southern Caribbean and Kekoldi

Caribbean lowland forest, reef coast and the second biggest raptor passage on Earth, four hours from San Jose

The coast southeast of Puerto Limon runs from Cahuita's reef down to the Panama border, and the Talamanca mountains crowd it into a narrow strip. That funnel is why Kekoldi counts raptors in the millions every autumn: Turkey Vultures, Broad-winged and Swainson's Hawks and Mississippi Kites make up almost the whole flight, and the watch sits on Bribri and Cabecar land above Puerto Viejo. Outside passage the draw is lowland forest that meets the sea, which is a habitat no other region above has.

  • Habitat: A low ridge between the Talamanca mountains and the Caribbean at 0 to 200 m, which funnels the whole raptor migration into a corridor a few kilometres wide.
  • When: The raptor passage runs through October and November, and again in March. Over two million raptors are counted here in a season, among the top three watches in the world.
  • Getting there: From Puerto Viejo de Talamanca head north for 4 km and turn left onto a dirt road by a small store. Reservations with the Kekoldi reserve are required and a guide walks you up.
  • Look for: Turkey Vulture, Broad-winged Hawk, Swainson's Hawk, Mississippi Kite, Snowy Cotinga, Semiplumbeous Hawk, Purple-throated Fruitcrow, Montezuma Oropendola
  • Also recorded in the parks here: Black-capped Pygmy Tyrant, Nicaraguan Seed Finch
  • Parks and reserves:
    • Cahuita National Park, A coastal park entered at Kelly Creek on a donation basis. A flat trail runs between forest and beach.
    • Gandoca-Manzanillo National Wildlife Refuge
  • Stops:
    • : A viewing platform on the Kekoldi indigenous reserve ridge above Puerto Viejo, visited with a local guide. The raptor passage crosses here in September, October and November.
    • : The coast road south through beach forest to the Gandoca refuge, birded on foot or by bike. Snowy Cotinga sits on the treetops here.
    • : Mangrove and lagoon at the Panama border inside the Gandoca-Manzanillo refuge. Reach it on foot or by boat.
  • Also covers: Cahuita National Park, Gandoca lagoon, Gandoca-Manzanillo National Wildlife Refuge, Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, Punta Uva and Manzanillo, The Kekoldi hawk watch
  • Also watch for: Cahuita's reef is the best developed on the Costa Rican Caribbean and is snorkelled from the beach. Three-toed sloth, mantled howler and white-faced capuchin are all routine along the park trail, and green and hawksbill turtles nest at Gandoca from March to July.

Carara and the Tarcoles River

Where the dry northwest meets the wet south, 90 minutes from San Jose

Carara sits on the transition between two forest types, so a single morning walk covers species from both. The boat trip on the Tarcoles adds mangrove specialties, and Scarlet Macaws commute overhead at dawn and dusk.

  • Habitat: A transition zone at sea level where tropical dry forest meets tropical wet forest on the south bank of the Tárcoles, so both faunas live side by side.
  • When: December to April for the dry season and the scarlet macaws crossing to roost at dusk. The river boat works in every month.
  • Getting there: From the Route 23 junction take Route 34 south towards Jacó. The Tárcoles bridge is 11.2 km on and the park headquarters 2.4 km beyond it on the left.
  • Look for: Scarlet Macaw, Mangrove Hummingbird, Boat-billed Heron, Turquoise-browed Motmot
  • Also recorded in the parks here: Green Shrike-Vireo, Black-striped Woodcreeper, Streak-chested Antpitta, Black-headed Trogon, Streak-backed Oriole, Stripe-headed Sparrow
  • National parks: Carara National Park, La Cangreja National Park
  • Stops:
    • : A flat trail through an old river oxbow inside Carara National Park, entered at the main gate. This is transition forest and Baird's Trogon country.
    • : A two hour launch trip from the village of Tarcoles, run by several local operators and bookable on the day. Boat-billed Heron and the mangrove specialities come closer here than anywhere.
    • : The mangrove stand at the river mouth. A boat or a rough track gets you there, and this is where Mangrove Hummingbird is looked for.
    • : The roadside crocodile stop on the coastal road. It is also a useful place to scan for macaws crossing at dusk.
  • Also covers: Carara National Park, Guacalillo mangroves, La Cangreja National Park, The Meandrica trail, The Tarcoles bridge, The Tarcoles river boat
  • Also watch for: The Tárcoles bridge is the most reliable American crocodile viewpoint in the country, with large animals visible on the sandbanks at low water. White-faced capuchin and green iguana are constant along the park trails.

Manuel Antonio and the Quepos Coast

Pacific rainforest above the beaches, easy to reach

The national park is small, busy and full of wildlife, with sloths and monkeys along the main trail. The Santa Juana foothills behind the coast are quieter and hold the foothill species the park misses.

  • Habitat: Lush tropical forest at sea level running down to beaches, with mangrove and secondary growth outside the park boundary where most of the birding is.
  • When: December to April is the dry season and the busy one. The forest outside the park is quieter and better birding than the park itself.
  • Getting there: From Quepos follow the well-signed Manuel Antonio road southeast for 6 km over the hillside. Reserve accommodation well ahead in high season.
  • Look for: Fiery-billed Aracari, Baird's Trogon, Riverside Wren
  • Also recorded in the parks here: Chiriqui Foliage-gleaner, Turquoise Cotinga, Great Black Hawk, Band-tailed Barbthroat, Charming Hummingbird, White-crested Coquette, Black-hooded Antshrike
  • National parks:
    • Manuel Antonio National Park, A small coastal park with a daily visitor cap, booked through SICORE. It is best in the first hour after opening.
    • Marino Ballena National Park
  • Stops:
    • Rainmaker : A private reserve inland from Quepos, open for day visits. Its canopy walkway crosses a river gorge.
    • Hacienda Baru : A private reserve and lodge at Dominical with forest, mangrove and its own trails. It is quieter than the national park.
    • : Shore, river edge and beach scrub where the river meets the sea. Coastal migrants stop here.
  • Also covers: Hacienda Baru, Manuel Antonio National Park, Manuel Antonio, Quepos, Marino Ballena National Park, Rainmaker, The Savegre river mouth
  • Also watch for: Central American squirrel monkey lives only on this stretch of coast and in the Osa, and troops cross the park trails daily. Three-toed sloth and white-faced capuchin are both easy here.

The Osa Peninsula, Corcovado and Golfo Dulce

The most remote forest in the country

Osa holds the largest lowland rainforest left on the Pacific coast of Central America, with Scarlet Macaws in flocks and Black-cheeked Ant-Tanager, which lives here and nowhere else. Corcovado entry requires a licensed local guide, and the lodges around Drake Bay and the Golfo Dulce are reached by boat or a rough road.

  • Habitat: One of the largest expanses of primary lowland rainforest left in the Americas, 100,000 acres on the western edge of the peninsula. It holds over 350 species.
  • When: December to April, and the peninsula is wet even then. Access and trails are hardest from September to November.
  • Getting there: Reservations with the park office are required well in advance. Three primary entrances exist; the simplest is a chartered light aircraft directly to Sirena station on the shore.
  • Look for: Scarlet Macaw, Black-cheeked Ant-Tanager, White-crested Coquette, Yellow-billed Cotinga, Yellow-throated Toucan, King Vulture
  • Also recorded in the parks here: Baird's Trogon, Black-striped Woodcreeper, Rufous Piha, Turquoise Cotinga
  • National parks: Corcovado National Park, Piedras Blancas National Park
  • Stops:
    • : The remote station at the heart of Corcovado. It is reached by boat and needs a licensed guide and a booking.
    • : A pull-in on the road onto the peninsula, scanned at first light. It is the classic spot for Yellow-billed Cotinga over the mangroves.
    • : A public trail along the coast between the lodges. Walk it in either direction.
    • : Ridge forest above the gulf. The lodges that hold it are the way in, and this is Black-cheeked Ant-Tanager country.
  • Also covers: Agujitas de Drake, Cerro Osa and the Golfo Dulce forest, Corcovado National Park, Golfito, Piedras Blancas National Park, Puerto Jimenez, Sirena ranger station, Corcovado, The Drake Bay coastal path, The Rio Rincon bridge
  • Also watch for: All four Costa Rican monkey species live here, along with Baird's tapir and, with luck and patience, jaguar tracks. Humpback whales are in the Golfo Dulce from July to October and again from December to March.

Boca Tapada

Lowland rainforest on the San Carlos river, in the far north

The most reliable place in the country for Great Green Macaw, which nests in the almendro trees along the river. Lodges here run photography hides and river trips, and the surrounding forest holds the Caribbean lowland list without the crowds at Sarapiqui and La Selva.

Not on the three itineraries above. Add two nights between Arenal and Sarapiqui. It is a long drive on gravel for the last stretch, so it works as a detour from La Fortuna rather than a stop on the way to anywhere.

  • Habitat: Two hundred and fifty acres of primary lowland forest at 50 m, 15 km from the Nicaraguan border, with lagoons holding caiman and turtles and 15 km of flat, muddy trails.
  • When: December to April for the drier road. Great Green Macaws are on the almendro through the first half of the year.
  • Getting there: From Pital follow the main road until it turns to dirt at a filling station, then roughly 34 km of dirt through Boca Tapada. Fill up at the station and take a four-wheel drive.
  • Look for: Great Green Macaw, Great Curassow, Keel-billed Toucan, Snowy Cotinga, Semiplumbeous Hawk, Sunbittern, Rufous-winged Woodpecker
  • Parks and reserves: Maquenque National Wildlife Refuge
  • Stops:
    • : A lodge and private reserve. Its lagoon, almendro trees and feeder deck are open to day visitors, and Great Green Macaw nests here in season.
    • : A boat trip on the border river, arranged through the lodges. Kingfishers, Sungrebe and Sunbittern show from the water.
    • : A national wildlife refuge of lowland forest and lagoons. It is the quietest Caribbean lowland birding in the region.
  • Also covers: Laguna del Lagarto, Maquenque National Wildlife Refuge, Maquenque refuge trails, The San Carlos river boat
  • Also watch for: Spectacled caiman in the lagoons, two-toed sloth in the lodge grounds, and a strong dart frog list on the trails. The area is quiet enough that mammals show themselves more readily than on the busier routes.

San Vito and Coto Brus

Highland forest and a botanical garden at 1,200 metres, near the Panama border

The Wilson Botanical Garden anchors the birding here, with a highland list that overlaps neither the Talamanca oak forest above nor the Osa lowlands below. Coto Brus is the stronghold for several species that are hard anywhere else in Costa Rica.

Not on the three itineraries above. Add two or three nights on the way south to The Osa Peninsula, Corcovado and Golfo Dulce, or as the far end of a southern loop. It is the longest drive above from San Jose, so it suits a trip of two weeks or more.

  • Habitat: Six hundred and twenty-five acres of largely primary forest at 1,150 m, a textbook fragment in a landscape cleared for coffee, with a botanical garden at its centre.
  • When: December to April. The garden and the forest edge work through the day and the fragment is small enough to cover in one.
  • Getting there: From San Vito take Route 237 towards Ciudad Neily for 5.8 km and Las Cruces is on the right. Staying at the station itself is the simplest way to bird it.
  • Look for: Turquoise Cotinga, White-crested Coquette, Silvery-throated Jay, Fiery-billed Aracari, Spot-crowned Euphonia, Marbled Wood Quail, Black-thighed Grosbeak
  • National park: La Amistad International Park
  • Stops:
    • Wilson Botanical Garden : A botanical garden and research station run by the Organization for Tropical Studies, with rooms, a restaurant and trails. Almost everyone uses it as their base here.
    • : The block of primary forest behind the garden, on the same trail network. It holds the Chiriqui highland species.
    • : Marsh and pond edge below the town. It is a short drive for a completely different habitat.
  • Also covers: La Amistad International Park, Las Cruces forest reserve, San Vito, The Coto Brus wetlands, Wilson Botanical Garden
  • Also watch for: Agouti, coati and both squirrel species through the Wilson Botanical Garden, and the surrounding forest fragments hold olingo on night walks. Amphibians are at their most active from May to November.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the best time for birding in Costa Rica?

December to April brings dry Pacific weather with wintering migrants on top of the residents, and February to April is the heart of quetzal season. September and October are the Caribbean slope's calmest spell and carry the huge southbound raptor passage along that coast. The three seasons, and the best month for each headline bird.

Do I need a guide?

Costa Rica is one of the easiest countries in the tropics to bird independently: distances are short, the roads are good and the lodges are built for birders. A local guide will still find you far more, especially in cloud forest, and Corcovado National Park requires a licensed guide by law. Costa Rican operators selling day tours and guided birding. Your lodge is the other route to one: 15 of the 140 places to stay listed here include a guided activity in the rate, 44 offer birding as an activity you pay for separately, and 81 publish nothing either way, which each card prints rather than leaving blank.

Are the parks free to enter?

No. National parks charge foreign visitors an entry fee, and several also cap daily numbers and have to be booked ahead through SICORE, SINAC's own reservation system. Poas, Irazu, Rincon de la Vieja, Carara, Manuel Antonio, Chirripo, Tapanti, Los Quetzales and both Tortuguero sectors are all on that system. Corcovado additionally requires a licensed local guide. The private reserves that matter most to birders, Monteverde and La Selva among them, sit outside the state system and set their own fees and their own guide rules. Entry sits outside the room rate everywhere: of the 113 places to stay here that publish what the rate covers, none includes a park fee, so budget it per park per day and pay at the gate or through SICORE.

Can I drive myself, and do I need a 4x4?

Yes, and it is one of the pleasures of birding here. Main roads are good and distances are short. Almost everyone collects the car at Juan Santamaria airport outside San Jose, the SJO arrivals hall, where the international and Costa Rican firms all have desks; Liberia airport in the northwest is the other pickup point and suits a trip that starts in Guanacaste, Tenorio and the northern wetlands. Take a 4x4 for the steep approaches to Monteverde, the Dota valley and The Osa Peninsula, Corcovado and Golfo Dulce. Tortuguero is the exception: it is reached by boat or light aircraft, so arrange that transfer rather than driving to it. Mandatory local liability insurance is charged at the desk on top of the headline rate, so read the quote before you compare prices. If you would rather leave the driving to somebody else, ask the lodge when you book the room. 6 of the properties listed here state a transfer in the rate, and they are the ones reached by boat or light aircraft, where the journey is part of the stay. Everywhere else a lodge will book you onto a shared shuttle or arrange a private transfer, and the two networks that carry most of that traffic are named below.

What does a two week trip cost?

Thirteen nights, before international flights. These are the lines that move.

  • Lodges: $80 to $150 a night mid-range, $100 to $300 mid-luxury, $180 to $500 luxury, $400 to $1,000 ultra-luxury. That is per room, so a solo traveller carries the whole of it.
  • Car: A compact 4x4 runs $55 to $85 a day, about $770 to $1,190 for the fortnight.
  • Fuel: The classic loop is about 567 km, so one to two tanks. Under $100 for the trip.
  • Guides: A guided morning with a local guide is $25 to $95, and will find you far more than you will find alone.
  • Meals: Many mid-range lodges include all of them, which removes the food line entirely, so check before you budget for it.

At the mid-range tier that lands at roughly $2,000 to $3,600 for one person travelling alone, or $1,050 to $2,000 each for two sharing, because the room, the car and the fuel all split. A fully guided group trip is a different shape at $250 to $600 per person per day, so $3,500 to $8,400 each for the fortnight, with everything above already inside it. Every place to stay with its published nightly rate, inside its region.

How many species can I expect to see?

The national list stands at 944. A thorough two to three week trip tops 400 species, and even a relaxed week built around three or four lodges commonly passes 250. Every bird above carries a collector card.

Which birds are found only in Costa Rica?

Seven, and three of them live 550 kilometres offshore. On the mainland there are four. Coppery-headed Emerald is the one most trips get, on the Caribbean slope at middle elevations around The Central Highlands and again at Monteverde, and it comes to feeders. Cabanis's Ground Sparrow holds the Central Valley scrub and the coffee edges around Turrialba and the Pacuare Valley, which is the only region above that reliably has it. Black-cheeked Ant Tanager lives on The Osa Peninsula, Corcovado and Golfo Dulce and nowhere else on earth, so the Osa is the trip that gets it. Mangrove Hummingbird needs Pacific mangrove, and the stands at Guacalillo near Carara and the Tarcoles River and around the Golfo Dulce are where to look.

The other three, Cocos Cuckoo, Cocos Tyrannulet and Cocos Finch, live on Cocos Island alone. It is a national park 550 kilometres out in the Pacific, reached by a liveaboard dive boat over about 36 hours each way, and no birding itinerary on this page goes there. A four endemic mainland trip is the realistic target, and getting all four means the Osa, the Pacific mangroves and the Caribbean slope in one route, which is what the Full Sweep does.

Is it worth going out at night?

Yes, and it is the part of a Costa Rican trip most visitors skip. A night walk on lodge trails is how you get Pauraque off the track ahead of you, Great Potoo on a bare snag, and the owls that stay invisible by day: Spectacled Owl and Crested Owl in lowland forest, Black-and-white Owl around lit clearings and town edges, and Costa Rican Pygmy Owl calling in the middle of the afternoon on the Caribbean slope, which is the one that breaks the rule. Ask at the desk when you check in, because most lodges run a guided night walk on their own trails for a small fee and it is rarely advertised in advance.

Two hours after dusk is the window. Bring a head torch with a red setting, walk slowly, and let the guide use the light rather than sweeping it yourself. On playback, the private reserves and the state parks set their own rules and several ban it outright in the breeding season; a resident guide knows which, and at a feeder or a known nest the answer is to sit still instead.

What is an army ant swarm, and how do I find one?

It is the best thing that can happen to a morning in lowland forest. A swarm of army ants drives insects up out of the leaf litter and a following flock of birds takes them, which brings species down to eye level that are otherwise a rumour in the canopy. Ocellated Antbird, Bicolored Antbird and Spotted Antbird are the professionals that live off swarms, and Northern Barred Woodcreeper and Grey-headed Tanager join them. Sarapiqui and La Selva, Tortuguero, The Osa Peninsula, Corcovado and Golfo Dulce and Boca Tapada are where it happens most.

You find one by listening. The birds are noisy and the sound carries further than the ants do, so a guide who stops walking and turns their head is worth the fee for this alone. A swarm moves slowly enough to stay with for an hour. Stand still at the edge and let it come past you, because walking into it moves the birds and gets you bitten.

What should I bring?

Binoculars first, and 8x42 suits most people here: the forest is close and often dark, so bright, easy binoculars beat powerful ones. A telescope is worth carrying only for the Tarcoles boat and the Guanacaste, Tenorio and the Northern Wetlands wetlands, and you can happily travel without one. Rubber boots matter more than you would expect, and most lowland lodges lend them, so ask before buying. Rain gear that folds small beats a heavy coat, because the rain arrives in the afternoon and passes. Take a fleece and a hat for San Gerardo de Dota and the Talamanca Highlands, where the paramo sits above 3,000 metres and mornings start close to freezing.

The field guide is Garrigues and Dean, The Birds of Costa Rica: A Field Guide, which is the one guides in the country carry. Learning its plates before you fly makes a real difference. A head torch with a red setting, a dry bag for your optics on boat days, and insect repellent for the Caribbean lowlands finish the list.

Where does the bird photography happen?

At feeders, at hides and on the water, far more than on the trail. Lodge hummingbird feeders and fruit tables are set up for it across The Central Highlands, Monteverde and Turrialba and the Pacuare Valley, and several lodges run purpose-built hides where you pay for a half day sitting still. The Carara and the Tarcoles River boat and the Tortuguero canals both put you at eye level with herons and kingfishers from a stable platform, which is the shot a trail rarely gives you.

Can I bird here with limited mobility?

Much of the best birding in Costa Rica happens without a hard walk. A great deal of it is done from lodge feeders and balconies, from boats on the Tortuguero canals and the Tarcoles River, and from the car on quiet roads. Several reserves keep flat, well surfaced trails, and the hanging bridge circuits at Arenal and Monteverde are graded rather than stepped. The genuinely demanding parts are optional: the 500 steps down to the La Fortuna waterfall, the steeper highland trails above San Gerardo de Dota, and Corcovado, which is a long hike in heat. Cloud forest mornings are cold, so bring a layer. Boat and feeder based regions. For accessibility detail before you book, the Birdability Map records step free access, surface, gradient, seating and accessible toilets at birding sites; it is crowd sourced and much stronger in the United States than in Costa Rica, so treat a blank area as unrecorded rather than unsuitable, and ask the lodge directly. Their Access Considerations guide is the best list of questions to ask.

What are the visa and health requirements?

Entry rules depend on your nationality, so there is no single answer, but there are directories that cover every country. Many nationalities are admitted visa free for up to 180 days. Check yours against your own government travel advice, for example the UK FCDO entry requirements page, or a nationality aware tool such as Sherpa. For health, two directories publish a page for every destination and are free to read: CDC Travelers Health and TravelHealthPro. Routine vaccinations cover most travellers, and dengue precautions are worth taking in the lowlands.

How far ahead should I book?

The lodges that fill first are the small ones in the places birders want most. Monteverde and San Gerardo de Dota go earliest, and the peak window from December to April is the one that sells out, so aim to hold rooms three to six months ahead for a February or March trip. The green season from May to August is far more forgiving and can often be built a few weeks out. Guides book on the same rhythm as the lodges, so ask for a guide when you hold the room rather than after you arrive.

Can I do this without driving?

Yes, and plenty of birders do. Two networks cover it.

  • Shared shuttles: Door to door minibuses run between every place on this page, and Interbus holds a Costa Rica CST certification. Slower than driving and far cheaper than a private transfer.
  • Domestic flights: Sansa flies San Jose to Drake Bay, Puerto Jimenez, Tortuguero, Golfito, Quepos, Nosara and Tamarindo, which turns the long southern legs of the full sweep from a day of driving into under an hour.
  • Lodge transfers: Most lodges will arrange the pickup themselves, and for Tortuguero that is the only way in, so it is arranged for you either way.

The trade off is flexibility: roadside stops and dawn starts at your own pace are the reason most birders take the car.
